passage: Session note, fourth meeting. Hafsa and Kashish said that arguments with Kashish's parents keep circling back to money advice: what to put savings into, when to buy a flat. Hafsa said aloud, "If we stop arguing about the advice, we lose nothing. If we keep arguing, we lose the visits." Kashish agreed and added, "It isn't perfect. They may feel we're shutting them out." Together they decided to keep money out of talks with the parents, keep visits to a couple of hours, and end each one with tea and a warm goodbye. I asked what they would do if the parents raised the subject; they planned to say, "We've got it handled, tell us about your week." Neither called this a permanent fix. Both said it would do for now and agreed to review it next time. I offered no views on their finances.

passage:
Sunday night

Another lunch at Chetan's parents' place, another lecture about money. Why do we rent instead of buying. Why did we buy a sofa. Why aren't we putting everything into gold like Mamaji's family.
On the drive home, Chetan and I finally talked about it properly. We can't change how his parents think. We've tried three times, and each time ended with his father upset and me in tears in the car.
So here's what we decided. Money is off the table at their house. If they bring it up, Chetan will say, gently, "We've got it sorted, Papa. How's your knee?" And we'll keep visits shorter: lunch and tea, not the whole day. Warm, polite, but shorter.
It isn't perfect. I don't love feeling like we're hiding. But it protects us, and it keeps us going there with a smile.
Good enough for now.
— Bidisha

How does Bidisha feel about the compromise?
qa.a: Bidisha feels relieved that it protects the marriage but also a bit uneasy, not loving the feeling of hiding.

qa.q: What else could Bidisha and Chetan try later if things settle?
qa.a: They could invite Chetan's parents to share one piece of advice they value, listening kindly without agreeing to change their plans.

qa.q: How might Chetan's parents experience the shorter, warmer visits?
qa.a: They may miss the long days and their money talks, but warm, relaxed visits could feel better than tense ones.

grounding: It shows a couple, after repeated conflicts over money advice, choosing to keep certain topics off-limits and visits short but warm as an imperfect compromise.

Pranav: so what are you going to do?
Sahil: we talked last night. we're not going to convince him. and every fight makes Megha feel she has to choose between us and her parents
Sahil: so: money is not a topic at their place anymore. if he raises it, I say "thank you, we've got a plan" and ask about his garden
Pranav: and visits?
Sahil: shorter. lunch, chai, leave by 4. but warm
Pranav: does that feel right?
Sahil: not fully. it's a bit like building a wall. but a small, polite wall is better than a fight every month
Pranav: fair 🙂
